items.question: Why do you want to keep building AI models that push the frontier?
items.object: Frontier AI models
items.answer: I think we always want to have models that are at the frontier or pushing the frontier because that's where you see what capabilities now exist that didn't exist at the slightly less capable last year's version or last six months ago version.
quotes: I think we always want to have models that are at the frontier or pushing the frontier because that's where you see what capabilities now exist that didn't exist at the slightly less capable last year's version or last six months ago version.

rubrics.text: The response identifies discovering capabilities absent from earlier, less capable models as a reason to build frontier AI models.

items.question: Why do you see building high-end frontier models and smaller, affordable models as complementary priorities?
items.object: Frontier models and smaller, affordable models
items.answer: We know those frontier models are going to be really useful for a bunch of use cases, but they're going to be a bit slower and a bit more expensive than people might like for a bunch of other broader use cases. So I think what we want to do is always have a highly capable, affordable model that enables a whole bunch of lower latency use cases. People can use them for agentic coding much more readily. And then have the high-end frontier model that is really useful for deep reasoning, solving really complicated math problems, those kinds of things. It's not that one or the other is useful. They're both useful. So I think we like to do both. And also, through distillation, which is a key technique for making the smaller models more capable, you have to have the frontier model in order to then distill it into your smaller model. So it's not an either-or choice. You need that in order to actually get a highly capable, more modest size model.
quotes: At the same time, we know those are going to be really useful for a bunch of use cases, but they're going to be a bit slower and a bit more expensive than people might like for a bunch of other broader use cases.

So I think what we want to do is always have a highly capable, affordable model that enables a whole bunch of lower latency use cases. People can use them for agentic coding much more readily. And then have the high-end frontier model that is really useful for deep reasoning, solving really complicated math problems, those kinds of things. It's not that one or the other is useful. They're both useful. So I think we like to do both.

And also, through distillation, which is a key technique for making the smaller models more capable, you have to have the frontier model in order to then distill it into your smaller model. So it's not an either-or choice. You need that in order to actually get a highly capable, more modest size model.

rubrics.text: The response identifies demand for low-latency applications as a reason to develop smaller models alongside frontier models.
The response explains that frontier models enable the development of more capable smaller models through distillation.

items.question: How do you understand the original motivation for model distillation?
items.object: The original motivation for model distillation
items.answer: I think distillation was originally motivated because we were seeing that we had a very large image data set at the time, 300 million images that we could train on with, I forget, like 20,000 categories or something, so much bigger than ImageNet. And we were seeing that if you create specialists for different subsets of those image categories, this one's going to be really good at mammals and this one's going to be really good at indoor room scenes or whatever, and you can cluster those categories and train on an enriched stream of data after you do pre-training on a much broader set of images. You get much better performance if you then treat that whole set of maybe 50 models you've trained as a large ensemble. But that's not a very practical thing to serve.
quotes: I think distillation was originally motivated because we were seeing that we had a very large image data set at the time, 300 million images that we could train on with, I forget, like 20,000 categories or something, so much bigger than ImageNet.

And we were seeing that if you create specialists for different subsets of those image categories, this one's going to be really good at mammals and this one's going to be really good at indoor room scenes or whatever, and you can cluster those categories and train on an enriched stream of data after you do pre-training on a much broader set of images.

items.question: How do you see distillation contributing to merging model capabilities without losing existing capabilities?
items.object: Distillation for merging model capabilities without loss
items.answer: I feel like some part of that whole capability merging without loss should be a distillation process, but I can't quite articulate it. I haven't seen much papers about it.

items.question: Why do you see distillation as a sweet spot for getting high performance from smaller models?
items.object: Distillation for improving smaller models
items.answer: With distillation, you can coax the right behavior out of the smaller model that you wouldn't otherwise get with just the hard labels. I think that's what we've observed: you can get very close to your largest model performance with distillation approaches. That seems to be a nice sweet spot for a lot of people.
quotes: Coax the right behavior out of the smaller model that you wouldn't otherwise get with just the hard labels.

items.question: What performance standard do you want to keep pursuing for each new generation of Gemini Flash?
items.object: The performance goal for successive generations of Gemini Flash
items.answer: As good or even substantially better than the previous generation's Pro. I think we're going to keep trying to do that because that seems like a good trend to follow.

Some are our Pro scale model, and we can distill from that into our Flash scale model. It's an important set of capabilities to have, and inference time scaling can also be a useful thing to improve the capabilities of a model.

items.question: Why do you think low latency is an important advantage of the Flash model?
items.object: The Flash model’s low latency
items.answer: One of the things quite nice about the Flash model is not only is it more affordable, it's also lower latency. And I think latency is actually a pretty important characteristic for these models because we're going to want models to do much more complicated things that are going to involve generating many more tokens from when you ask the model to do something until it actually finishes what you ask it to do, because you're going to ask now not just, "Write me a for loop," but, "Write me a whole software package to do X or Y or Z." Having low latency systems that can do that seems really important, and Flash is one way of doing that.

items.question: How do you think about the value of pushing AI model capabilities further as cheaper models become good enough for people's current tasks?
items.object: Demand for more capable AI models as cheaper models improve
items.answer: I think that's true if your distribution of what people are asking the models to do is stationary, right? But I think what often happens is as the models become more capable, people ask them to do more. This happens in my own usage. I used to try our models a year ago for some sort of coding task, and it was okay at some simpler things but wouldn't do work very well for more complicated things. Since then we've improved dramatically on the more complicated coding tasks, and now I'll ask it to do much more complicated things. I think that's true not just of coding, but now: can you analyze all the renewable energy deployments in the world and give me a report on solar panel deployment or whatever? That's a much more complicated task than people would have asked a year ago.

items.question: How do you judge when a public AI benchmark is useful for improving models?
items.object: Public benchmarks for evaluating AI models
items.answer: I think benchmarks, particularly external ones that are publicly available, have their utility, but they often have a lifespan of utility where they're introduced and maybe they're quite hard for current models. I like to think the best kinds of benchmarks are ones where the initial scores are like 10 to 20 or 30 percent, maybe, but not higher. Then you can work on improving that capability for whatever it is the benchmark is trying to assess and get it up to like 80, 90 percent, whatever. Once it hits 95 percent or something, you get very diminishing returns from really focusing on that benchmark because it's either the case that you've now achieved that capability, or there's also the issue of leakage in public data or very related data being in your training data.

items.question: How do you use held-out internal benchmarks to guide improvements in model capabilities?
items.object: Held-out internal benchmarks for developing model capabilities
items.answer: So we have a bunch of held-out internal benchmarks that we really look at where we know that wasn't represented in the training data at all. There are capabilities that we want the model to have that it doesn't have now, and then we can work on assessing how do we make the model better at these kinds of things? items.question: How do you think about whether an architectural change suggested by a benchmark is worth making?
items.object: Architectural changes motivated by benchmarks
items.answer: I think the more meta lesson level I'm trying to operate at here is: you have a benchmark, you're like, okay, I see the architectural thing I need to do in order to go fix that, but should you do it? Because sometimes that's an inductive bias, basically. You're going to win short term; longer term, I don't know if that's going to scale. You might have to undo that.

items.question: What would you want long-context AI models to be capable of?
items.object: Long-context capabilities in AI models
items.answer: I mean, I like to sort of not focus on exactly what solution one should drive, but what capability would you want? I think we're very convinced that long context is useful, but it's way too short today. What you would really want is, can I attend to the internet while I answer my question? But that's not going to be solved by purely scaling the existing solutions, which are quadratic. A million tokens kind of pushes what you can do. You're not going to do that to a trillion tokens, let alone, you know, a billion tokens, let alone a trillion. But I think if you could give the illusion that you can attend to trillions of tokens, that would be amazing. You'd find all kinds of uses for that. You would attend to the internet. You could attend to the pixels of YouTube and the deeper representations that we can form for a single video, but across many videos. On a personal Gemini level, you could attend to all of your personal state, with your permission, so your emails, your photos.

items.question: How do you think an LLM system should identify the relevant information when working across trillions of tokens?
items.object: Hierarchical retrieval for LLM systems attending to internet-scale information
items.answer: I think even pre-language-model-based work, our ranking systems would be built to start with a giant number of web pages in our index. Many of them are not relevant, so you identify a subset of them that are relevant with very lightweight kinds of methods. Now you're down to like 30,000 documents or something, and then you gradually refine that to apply more and more sophisticated algorithms and signals of various kinds, in order to get down to ultimately what you show, which is the final 10 results or 10 results plus other kinds of information. An LLM-based system is not going to be that dissimilar, right? You're going to attend to trillions of tokens, but you're going to want to identify what are the 30,000-ish documents with maybe 30 million interesting tokens, and then how do you go from that into what are the 117 documents I really should be paying attention to in order to carry out the task the user has asked me to do? You can imagine systems where you have a lot of highly parallel processing to identify those initial 30,000 candidates, maybe with very lightweight kinds of models. Then you have some system that helps you narrow down from 30,000 to the 117 with maybe a little bit more sophisticated model or set of models. And then maybe the final model is the thing that looks at 117 things. That might be your most capable model. I think it has to be some system like that that really enables you to give the illusion of attending to trillions of tokens, sort of the way Google Search gives you—not the illusion, but you are searching the internet. But you're finding a very small subset of things that are relevant.

items.question: How did you arrive at the decision to put Google's entire search index in memory in 2001?
items.object: Google's 2001 decision to put its entire search index in memory
items.answer: One of the things that really happened in 2001 was we were working to scale the system in multiple dimensions. One is we wanted to make our index bigger so we could retrieve from a larger index, which always helps your quality in general, because if you don't have the page in your index, you're not going to do well. And then we also needed to scale our capacity because our traffic was growing quite extensively. We had a sharded system where you have more and more shards as the index grows. You have like 30 shards, and then if you want to double the index size you make 60 shards, so that you can bound the latency by which you respond for any particular user query. Then as traffic grows, you add more and more replicas of each of those. We eventually did the math and realized that in a data center where we had, say, 60 shards and 20 copies of each shard, we now had 1,200 machines with disks. We did the math and were like, hey, one copy of that index would actually fit in memory across 1,200 machines. So in 2001 we introduced—we put our entire index in memory.

So in 2001 we introduced—we put our entire index in memory.

items.question: How do you think a hundredfold increase in scale changes the way you should design a system?
items.object: System design under a hundredfold increase in scale
items.answer: If I design a system for X and something suddenly becomes 100X, that would enable a very different point in the design space that would not make sense at X, but all of a sudden 100X makes total sense. Going from a disk-based index to an in-memory index makes a lot of sense once you have enough traffic, because now you have enough replicas of the sort of state on disk that those machines can actually hold a full copy of the index in memory. And that all of a sudden enables a completely different design that wouldn't have been practical before.

items.question: How do you think programmers should use the basic latency numbers in “Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know” when designing software?
items.object: “Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know” and back-of-the-envelope system design
items.answer: I think this gets to the point of being able to do these back-of-the-envelope calculations. These are the raw ingredients of those, and you can use them to say, okay, well, if I need to design a system to do image search and thumbnailing of the result page, how might I do that? I could precompute the image thumbnails. I could try to thumbnail them on the fly from the larger images. What would that do? How much disk bandwidth do I need? How many disk seeks would I do? You can do thought experiments in 30 seconds or a minute with the basic numbers at your fingertips. As you build software using higher-level libraries, you want to develop the same intuitions for how long does it take to look up something in this particular kind of hash table I use, or how long will it take me to sort a million numbers?

items.question: How do you think about the energy costs that make batching important for AI accelerators?
items.object: Energy costs of data movement and batching in AI accelerators
items.answer: I think it's really good to think about calculations you're doing in a model, either for training or inference. Often a good way to view that is how much state will you need to bring in from memory, either on-chip SRAM or HBM from the accelerator-attached memory or DRAM or over the network? And then how expensive is that data motion relative to the cost of, say, an actual multiply in the matrix multiply unit? And that cost is actually really, really low, right? Depending on your precision, I think it's like sub-pico, one picojoule. I mean, it's all going to be about energy and how do you make the most energy efficient. Moving data from the SRAM on the other side of the chip—not even off-chip, but on the other side of the same chip—can be a thousand picojoules. This is why your accelerators require batching, because if you move, say, the parameter of a model from SRAM on the chip into the multiplier unit, that's going to cost you a thousand picojoules. So you better make use of that thing that you moved many, many times. That's where the batch dimension comes in, because if you have a batch of 256 or something, that's not so bad. But if you have a batch of one, that's really not good.

items.question: Why do you think collaboration between TPU chip designers and machine learning researchers is important for designing future hardware?
items.object: Co-designing future TPUs with machine learning researchers
items.answer: We have a lot of interaction between the TPU chip design architecture team and the higher-level modeling experts, because we really want to take advantage of being able to co-design what future TPUs should look like based on where we think the ML research puck is going, in some sense. As a hardware designer for ML in particular, you're trying to design a chip starting today, and that design might take two years before it even lands in a data center. Then it has to have a reasonable lifetime of three, four, or five years. So you're trying to predict two to six years out what ML computations people will want to run. Having people with interesting ML research ideas of things we think will start to work in that time frame, or will be more important in that time frame, really enables us to get interesting hardware features put into TPU N plus two, where TPU N is what we have today.

items.question: How do you judge whether an experimental feature is worth including in a future TPU design?
items.object: Speculative features and major changes in TPU design
items.answer: Sometimes you can squeeze some changes into N plus one, but bigger changes are going to require the chip design be earlier in its lifetime design process. Whenever we can do that, it's generally good. Sometimes you can put in speculative features that maybe won't cost you much chip area, but if they work out, it would make something 10 times as fast. If they don't work out, you burned a tiny amount of your chip area on that thing, but it's not that big a deal. Sometimes it's a very big change, and we want to be pretty sure this is going to work out, so we'll do lots of careful ML experimentation to show us this is actually the way we want to go.

items.question: What makes research into the limitations of current AI models intellectually interesting to you?
items.object: AI research into the limitations of current models
items.answer: The nice thing about this field is there's lots and lots of smart people thinking about creative solutions to some of the problems that we all see, because everyone sees that the models are great at some things and they fall down around the edges of those things, and are not as capable as we'd like in those areas. Coming up with good techniques and trying those and seeing which ones actually make a difference is what the whole research aspect of this field is pushing forward. I think that's why it's super interesting.

items.question: Why does handling symbolic reasoning within neural-net-based models make more sense to you than using separate symbolic systems?
items.object: Neural-net-based reasoning versus separate symbolic systems
items.answer: I think it makes a lot of sense to me, because humans manipulate symbols, but we probably don't have a symbolic representation in our heads. We have some distributed representation that is neural-net-like in some way, of lots of different neurons and activation patterns firing when we see certain things, and that enables us to reason and plan and do chains of thought and roll them back. That approach for solving the problem doesn't seem like it's going to work; I'm going to try this one. In a lot of ways, we're emulating what we intuitively think is happening inside real brains in neural-net-based models. So it never made sense to me to have completely separate discrete symbolic things and then a completely different way of thinking about those things.

items.question: How would you prefer Gemini to use your personal information?
items.object: Personalizing Gemini through retrieval
items.answer: We're not going to train Gemini on my email. We'd rather have a single model that we can use and use retrieval from my email as a tool, have the model reason about it and retrieve from my photos or whatever, make use of that, and have multiple stages of interaction.

items.question: How do you see the value of domain-specific models built on a general base model like Gemini?
items.object: Domain-specific models and the data trade-offs involved in specializing Gemini
items.answer: I think vertical models are interesting. You want them to start from a pretty good base model, but you can view them as enriching the data distribution for that particular vertical domain. For healthcare, say, or robotics, we're probably not going to train Gemini on all possible robotics data. We could train it on that, but we wanted to have a balanced set of capabilities. We'll expose it to some robotics data, but if you're trying to build a really, really good robotics model, you're going to want to start with that and then train it on more robotics data. Maybe that would hurt its multilingual translation capability but improve its robotics capabilities. We're always making these trade-offs in the data mix we train the base Gemini models on. We'd love to include data from 200 more languages and as much data as we have for those languages. But that's going to displace some other capabilities of the model. It won't be as good at Perl programming. It'll still be good at Python programming because we'll include enough of that, but there are other long-tail computer languages or coding capabilities that it may suffer on, or multimodal reasoning capabilities may suffer because we didn't expose it to as much data there. But it's really good at multilingual things.

items.question: How would you like specialized capabilities to work together with a general base model?
items.object: Modular models that combine specialized capabilities with a general base model
items.answer: I think some combination of specialized models, maybe more modular models, would be nice: the capability to have those 200 languages plus this awesome robotics model plus this awesome healthcare module that all can be knitted together to work in concert and called upon in different circumstances. If I have a health-related thing, then it should enable using this health module in conjunction with the main base model to be even better at those kinds of things. Some of that installable stuff can come from retrieval, but some of it probably should come from training on 100 billion tokens or a trillion tokens of health data.

items.question: How do you think about the different kinds of progress needed to scale neural networks effectively?
items.object: Scaling neural networks through hardware, software, and algorithmic improvements
items.answer: Combining a lot of those techniques and really trying to push on scaling things up over the last 15 years has been really important. That means improvements in the hardware, pushing on building specialized hardware like TPUs. It also means pushing on software abstraction layers to let people express ML ideas effectively. And then also working on things like sparse models. I've felt for a long time that sparsely activated models are really important because you want the models to have a lot of capacity, to our earlier discussion about remembering a lot of stuff. But you also want to be super efficient in how you activate your models. You'd like trillions of parameters, but activate only 1%, 5%, or 10% of that. We did an early paper on this where we scaled up outrageously large neural networks. The title, I think, is Noam's wording, which is a good catchy title. That gave you a 10x improvement in time to quality or compute cost to a given quality level relative to non-sparse models. Transformers similarly gave you a 10x to 100x improvement in compute cost to a given quality level versus LSTMs at the time. All of those things multiply together. All those things are important to work on: hardware, systems infrastructure, algorithmic aspects of model architecture, improving the data, improving the RL recipes. All these things are stacking together and multiplying together.

items.question: How do you think about coordinating the large number of people contributing to Gemini models?
items.object: Coordinating the large Gemini team
items.answer: I think it's perfectly good to have actually a lot of co-authors. Organizing that number of people so that they're effectively pushing in common directions, and all their work multiplies together in the ultimate output, the next generation of model, is pretty tricky. We have awesome people throughout the Gemini team to help orchestrate this: myself, Noam, and Oriol are helping steer this, and then we have people thinking about what the pre-training setup looks like, the infrastructure, the post-training recipe, the data preparation and eval, multimodal capabilities, and coding capabilities. A lot of different areas are super important, and it's really good to have people paying close attention to those things and all the other things.

items.question: Why did you think Google should combine its separate AI model efforts into the Gemini effort?
items.object: Google's fragmentation of AI research resources and the origin of Gemini
items.answer: I actually wrote a one-page memo saying we were being stupid by fragmenting our resources. At the time, we had efforts within Google Research and the Brain team on large language models. We also had efforts on multimodal models in other parts of Brain and Google Research, and legacy DeepMind had efforts like Chinchilla models and Flamingo models. We were fragmenting not only our compute across those separate efforts but also our best people and our best ideas. I said this is just stupid. Why don't we combine things and have one effort to train an awesome single unified model that is multimodal from the start, that's good at everything? That was the origin of the Gemini effort, and my one-page memo worked, which is good.

items.question: How do you think software engineers should shape their interactions with AI coding models?
items.object: Interaction styles between software engineers and AI coding models
items.answer: The coding tools are getting vastly better compared to where they were a year or two ago. Now you can rely on them to do more complex things that you as a software engineer want to accomplish, and delegate pretty complex things to these tools. One really nice aspect about the interaction between a human software engineer and a coding model they're working with is your way of talking to that coding model dictates how it interacts with you. You could ask it, "Please write a bunch of good tests for this." You could ask it, "Please help me brainstorm performance ideas." Your way of doing that is going to shape how the model responds, what kinds of problems it tackles, how much you want the model to go off and do things that are larger and more independent versus interact with it more to make sure you're shaping the right kinds of things. It's not the case that any one style is right for everything. Some kinds of problems you want a more frequent interaction style with the model, and other ones you're like, "Yeah, please just go write this, because I know I need this thing. I can specify it well enough. Go off and do it and come back when you're done."

items.question: How do you see the coordination challenges of having many independent software agents working on your behalf?
items.object: Managing many independent AI software agents
items.answer: I think there's going to be more of a style of having lots of independent software agents off doing things on your behalf, and figuring out the right human-computer interaction model and UI for when it should interrupt you and say, "Hey, I need a little more guidance here," or, "I've done this thing; now what should I do?" We're not at the end-all answer to that question. As the models get better, the decisions you put into how the interaction should happen may change. If you have a team of 50 interns, how would you manage that if they were people? On the other hand, imagine a classical software organization without AI-assisted tools. You would have 50 people doing stuff, and their interaction style is naturally hierarchical because these 50 people are working on this part of the system and not interacting that much with other people over here. But if you have five people each managing 50 virtual agents, they might actually have much higher-bandwidth communication among the five people than five people who are also trying to coordinate a 50-person software team each.

items.question: How do you think general software engineering guides can help coding agents build better systems?
items.object: General software engineering guides as context for coding agents
items.answer: I think well-written guides on how to do good software engineering are going to be useful because they can be used as input to models or read by other developers, so that their prompts are more clear about what the underlying software system should be doing. It may not be that you need to create a custom one for every situation. If you have general guides and put those into the context of a coding agent, that can be helpful. You can imagine one for distributed systems: think about failures of these kinds of things, and here are some techniques you can use to deal with failures. You can have Paxos-like replication, or send the request to two places and tolerate failure because you only need one of them to come back. A little description of 20 techniques like that in building distributed systems would probably go a long way toward having a coding agent cobble up more reliable and robust distributed systems.

That's going to be really important for systems that need to do a lot of stuff between your interactions.

items.question: Why do you consider AI generation at 10,000 tokens per second a meaningful goal for specialized hardware?

items.answer: More and more specialized hardware is going to enable much lower-latency models and much more capable models for affordable prices than the current status quo. That's going to be quite important. Being able to do that at 10,000 tokens per second would be awesome. Because of chain-of-thought reasoning, you could do many more tokens. It may not end up with 10,000 tokens of code—a thousand tokens of code with 9,000 tokens of reasoning behind it, which would actually probably be much better code to read.
